items.title: Neurons don't 'fire harder' — they fire faster or not at all
items.claim: A neuron's action potential is all-or-nothing. The size of every action potential in a given neuron is essentially identical. Strong stimuli don't make bigger spikes — they make more spikes per second.

options.text: By the amplitude of each action potential
By the FREQUENCY of action potentials (and by the pattern of which neurons fire and when) — the rate code is the simplest model, but timing and synchrony also carry information
By the colour of the signal
By the chemical identity of each spike

items.reveal_title: Edgar Adrian and the discovery of the rate code
items.reveal:
Edgar Adrian (Nobel 1932) recorded from single sensory neurons in frogs and found: stretch a muscle and the neuron fires more spikes per second. Spike amplitude didn't change. The signal was the frequency.

Action potentials are regenerative — voltage-gated sodium channels self-amplify any membrane depolarisation past threshold into a stereotyped spike, then sodium channels inactivate and potassium channels repolarise. Sub-threshold stimuli produce no spike at all; supra-threshold stimuli produce one spike, of fixed size.

The brain reads intensity from spike rate, fine timing from spike intervals, and 'identity' from which neurons fired. Some neural systems (auditory, visual) encode information in spike timing to within a millisecond.
items.why: Sensory intensity feels continuous. The neuron encoding it is digital — and the continuous sensation is reconstructed from spike statistics.

items.title: Jellyfish swim and hunt with no brain
items.claim: A jellyfish has no central nervous system. Just a 'nerve net' distributed across its body. Yet it swims rhythmically, captures prey, navigates currents, and (in some species) processes visual information from 24 separate eyes.
items.prompt: How does a decentralised nervous system coordinate behaviour?

options.text: It doesn't really — jellyfish drift passively

Nerve nets are distributed neural networks where any neuron can communicate with neighbours in all directions; rhythmic pacemakers (rhopalia in many medusae) generate swimming signals that propagate across the bell
Jellyfish have a hidden tiny brain

items.reveal:
Cnidarians (jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, Hydra) are among the simplest animals with nervous systems. They have a nerve NET rather than centralised ganglia or a brain.

Nerves form a diffuse 2D network across the body wall. Many cnidarian neurons are 'bipolar' — propagating signals in either direction. The network has no obvious centre. Synapses are often non-polarised.

Despite the apparent simplicity, cnidarians produce coordinated behaviour:
- Rhythmic bell pulsations for swimming (governed by 'rhopalia' — small sensory clusters around the bell margin in most jellyfish).
- Coordinated tentacle action for prey capture.
- Light avoidance (Hydra), vertical migration (many planktonic jellyfish).
- Box jellyfish (Cubozoa) have 24 eyes in 4 'rhopalia' — including image-forming lensed eyes that probably do visual navigation around mangrove obstacles, despite no centralised processor.

The nerve net is evolutionarily ancestral. As bilaterians (most other animals) developed bilateral symmetry, they evolved centralised nervous systems (brains and ventral or dorsal nerve cords). Cnidarians stayed with the decentralised model and still do well.

Decentralised processing has appeared independently in some bilaterian groups too — echinoderms (starfish, sea urchins) have radial nerve cords without a brain.
items.why: Brains feel essential to animal behaviour. Jellyfish show how much can be done without one — distributed processing, rhythmic generators and sensory clusters can produce sophisticated behaviour.

items.title: Your core temperature varies by less than 1 degree all day
items.claim: Air temperature swings by 30 degrees C between Australian outback day and night. Sahara desert: 50 C day, 0 C night. Yet healthy human core temperature stays at 36.5-37.5 C across these extremes. We are walking thermostats.
items.prompt: How does the body hold core temperature constant?

options.text: The skin acts as insulation only

Negative feedback through the hypothalamus: sensors monitor core temperature; effectors include sweating (cooling), vasodilation/vasoconstriction (heat dump or retention), shivering (heat production), and behavioural responses (seek shade, put on clothes)
Body heat is generated constantly at the same rate

items.reveal:
The preoptic area of the hypothalamus contains warm-sensitive and cold-sensitive neurons. They integrate skin temperature (peripheral) and blood temperature (core) and adjust effector outputs.

When too hot: blood vessels in skin dilate; sweat glands release ~0.5-1.5 L/hour (up to 3 L/hour in heat-acclimated athletes); behaviour (seek shade).

When too cold: skin vessels constrict; shivering (involuntary skeletal muscle activity, heat output up to 5x resting); brown fat thermogenesis (less in adults); piloerection (goose bumps — useless on hairless humans but works in furred mammals); behaviour (seek shelter).

Fever is a deliberately raised set-point — the hypothalamus is told (by pyrogens) that 38.5 C is the new target. Your body now defends 38.5 the way it usually defends 37.

Heatstroke: thermoregulation fails at core temperatures above ~40 C. Mortality rises rapidly. Conversely, deep hypothermia (<30 C) shuts down cardiac function — but has been used surgically to extend safe ischemia times.

The set-point isn't constant: circadian variation (~0.5 C lower at night), menstrual cycle (~0.3 C higher post-ovulation), age-related decline in regulation precision.
items.why: Homeostasis is usually drawn as a circle on a board. It's an integration of dozens of mechanisms across the whole body — and breaks down in fascinating ways (fever, heatstroke, hypothermia) when stressed.
